caption:
Why can't we read the Indus script?

Mohenjo-daro was built around 2500 BCE on the lower Indus, in what is now Sindh, Pakistan. It was laid out on a grid. Waste water ran into covered drains along the main streets. Excavation has found over 700 wells — roughly one for every three houses, a density unheard of in Egypt or Mesopotamia at the time.

At its height perhaps 40,000 people lived there. By about 1700 BCE it was abandoned, along with the other big Indus cities. The ruins sat undocumented for around 3,700 years until R. D. Banerji visited in 1919–20; large-scale digging followed in 1924–25.

At Partition the finds were split. Some 12,000 objects were divided between India and Pakistan — in some cases literally, with necklaces and girdles having their beads separated into two piles. Pakistan asked for and received the Priest-King. India kept the small bronze Dancing Girl and the Pashupati seal.

What is still open: the script on the seals has never been deciphered, so the city's own name is unknown. Iravatham Mahadevan reads one seal as suggesting Kukkuṭārma, "city of the cockerel". Why the city was abandoned is still argued — repeated flooding, or land worn out by crops, pastures and brick-making. In 2012 Pakistani archaeologists warned that without better conservation the site could disappear by 2030.

Images: excavation photograph of Mohenjo-daro, 1924; the Pashupati seal; the bronze Dancing Girl photographed by Gary Todd; and two seal plates by Ernest Mackay. All public domain or CC0.
